doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

chapter: The Four Seasons and Bob Crewe
title: Four Lovers, Birdland and joining Bob Crewe's studio band
summary: He saw jazz in New York and Newark while the Four Lovers faded, then joined Bob Crewe's all-night studio band and learned pop music from him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: I have to write that comment down. “The triad band.” No sevenths allowed.

Yeah exactly. So although I learned that there was a different style of music that drew people, I still after work drove into New York, went to Birdland, you know saw Miles, Cannonball, Coltrane, Art Blakey. And there was also a jazz club in Newark called Sugar Hill and all the great jazz players came in. And I still followed, you know listened to jazz and was sort of drawn to do that. And in 1959 – well after The Four Lovers had their hit record Elvis became popular on RCA and The Four Lovers went on the back burner. So they lost their deal on RCA. We made a record when I was with The Four Lovers and we brought it to Bob Crewe. Bob Crewe ultimately became the producer of The Four Seasons. Bob had written “Silhouettes on the Shade,” he also produced Freddy Cannon. So he was already an established producer making hit records. And he asked us if we wanted to be his studio band. And he would pay us ten dollars apiece, and we would come in to the studio at 11 or 12:00 at night and work all night because he can get the studio free. So we started to make records and I got an opportunity to start to make records. Now being taught by Bob Crewe, who had hit records, was how I learned pop

music. He’d give me a record and say, “Charles I want the rhythm to sound like this. I want the horns to play this style, and I need strings. And here’s what I want the strings to do.” And he’d give me records to listen to.
